questions.knowledge_point: Expressing the Area Between Two Curves as an Integral by First Solving For the Limits of Integration
questions.problem: Which integral gives the area of the finite region bounded between $y=8{x}^{2}-4$ and $y=2-2x?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's draw a sketch of the two functions.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14033713/assets/b2f34492ce184169d0e720d5a2214a356236b56d6e20bd8ece584b967f074e64.png)

*(Note: Figure not drawn to scale)*

Now, we want to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we equate the two functions and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2-2x & =8{x}^{2}-4 \\ 8{x}^{2}+2x-6 & =0 \\ x & =\frac{-2\pm \sqrt{{2}^{2}-4\cdot 8\cdot (-6)}}{2\cdot 8} \\  & =\frac{-2\pm 14}{16}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=-1$ to $x=\frac{3}{4}.$

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, let's draw our vertical arrow.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14033713/assets/94243d27b465eca7957731385b2fe13fae36b811079d3077e2e093aa19d81ad3.png)

The vertical line 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y=8{x}^{2}-4,$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=2-2x.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{-1}^{3/4}[\,(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function})\,]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{3/4}[\,(2-2x)-(8{x}^{2}-4)\,]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{3/4}(-8{x}^{2}-2x+6)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which integral gives the area of the finite region bounded by $y=2{x}^{2}-3x$ and $y=5-2{x}^{2}-2x?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's draw a sketch of the two functions.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14033713/assets/9a4de823003f0461231c355a43ba9845358ec4a3767ca59c2ba2206456620373.png)

*(Note: Figure not drawn to scale)*

Now, we want to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we equate the two functions and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}-3x & =5-2{x}^{2}-2x \\ 4{x}^{2}-x-5 & =0 \\ x & =\frac{1\pm \sqrt{(-1)^{2}-4\cdot 4\cdot (-5)}}{2\cdot 4} \\  & =\frac{1\pm 9}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=-1$ to $x=\frac{5}{4}.$

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, let's draw our vertical arrow.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14033713/assets/94b0113f7ca9ffeca11398cce06995fa4a7e5cb3f39b3021d5d6ec56746b75ee.png)

The vertical line 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y=2{x}^{2}-3x,$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=5-2{x}^{2}-2x.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{-1}^{5/4}[\,(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function})\,]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{5/4}[\,(5-2{x}^{2}-2x)-(2{x}^{2}-3x)\,]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{5/4}(-4{x}^{2}+x+5)\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate the area of the finite region bounded by the curves $y=2{x}^{2}-2$ and $y=6.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's draw a sketch of the two functions.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14033713/assets/0fd8a89bdcad9f1b20c9fd35df9aa209a5e551d5d7a7c97f62103e23e7ae9741.png)

Now, we want to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we equate the two functions and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}-2 & =6 \\ 2{x}^{2} & =8 \\ {x}^{2} & =4 \\ x & =\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=-2$ to $x=2.$

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, we draw our vertical arrow.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14033713/assets/83e8d6af5284006b4caad6b1a96cb1298f7c7672d6c35fa652359d3a0b28e037.png)

The vertical line 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y=2{x}^{2}-2,$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=6.$

Therefore, we can find the area, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}[\,(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function})\,]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}[\,(6)-(2{x}^{2}-2)\,]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}(8-2{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(8x-\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3})|}_{-2}^{2} \\  & =[8\cdot 2-\frac{2}{3}\cdot {2}^{3}]-[8\cdot (-2)-\frac{2}{3}\cdot (-2)^{3}] \\  & =(16-\frac{16}{3})-(-16+\frac{16}{3}) \\  & =\frac{64}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate the area of the finite region bounded by the curves $y={x}^{2}-10$ and $y=6.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's draw a sketch of the two functions.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14033713/assets/9248483d8b55c2ac61fcc3c1f11fee0eabee92794eaacd1fb2e37fff68cec289.png)

Now, we want to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we equate the two functions and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-10 & =6 \\ {x}^{2} & =16 \\ x & =\pm 4\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=-4$ to $x=4.$

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, we draw our vertical arrow.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14033713/assets/173d726e4b0ecee37d8b7ca8878f5bc5934a069dc48a2b9d18e28d72f3b04f7e.png)

The vertical line 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y={x}^{2}-10,$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=6.$

Therefore, we can find the area, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{-4}^{4}[\,(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function})\,]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-4}^{4}[\,(6)-({x}^{2}-10)\,]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-4}^{4}(16-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(16x-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3})|}_{-4}^{4} \\  & =[16\cdot 4-\frac{1}{3}\cdot {4}^{3}]-[16\cdot (-4)-\frac{1}{3}\cdot (-4)^{3}] \\  & =(64-\frac{64}{3})-(-64+\frac{64}{3}) \\  & =\frac{256}{3}\end{aligned}
$$
